name: Dorchester
headline: Squares strung along the Red Line,
three-deckers between them, the Neponset at the edge.
answer: Dorchester is Boston's largest neighborhood, more than 6 square miles between South Boston and the Neponset River, founded as a separate town in 1630 and annexed to Boston in stages that ended in 1870. Its housing mixes single-family, two-family and three-decker homes and condominiums, and the Boston Planning & Development Agency counted 122,191 people there in 2020. Five Red Line stations, the Mattapan Line and Fairmount Line commuter rail stations including Uphams Corner, Four Corners/Geneva and Talbot Avenue serve it.
meta: Dorchester, Boston: three-deckers and Victorian houses around Fields Corner, Savin Hill, Codman Square and Lower Mills, on the Red Line and Fairmount Line.

boundaries.text: Dorchester is bordered by South Boston, the South End, Roxbury, Jamaica Plain and Hyde Park; the Neponset River separates it from Quincy and Milton, and Dorchester Bay lies to the east. It is often divided into North Dorchester, the part north of Quincy, East and Freeport Streets, and South Dorchester.

overview: Settlers who came on the Mary and John landed at Columbia Point in June 1630 and founded Dorchester months before Boston. The town held what is described as the first town meeting in what became the United States on October 8, 1633, buried its dead in the North Burying Ground at today's Uphams Corner from 1634, and opened the Mather School in 1639. Israel Stoughton built a grist mill on the Neponset River in 1634, and from 1765 chocolate was refined at Lower Mills, where the Walter Baker company made it until 1965. Boston took Dorchester in pieces, starting with Dorchester Neck (now South Boston) in 1804, and annexed the rest of the town in 1870.

Dorchester grew as a streetcar suburb. The Old Colony Railroad crossed it from 1845, Dorchester Avenue carried a horse-drawn streetcar, and by 1890 the streetcar and the three-decker had come together here, with three-deckers filling the land between the old village centers. Those centers are still the neighborhood's commercial squares: Uphams Corner and Bowdoin/Geneva in the north; Fields Corner, Codman Square, Peabody Square at Ashmont, Adams Village and Lower Mills to the south. The Red Line's Dorchester stations opened in 1927 and 1928, from Columbia (now JFK/UMass) through Savin Hill, Fields Corner and Shawmut to Ashmont.

Columbia Point, where the first settlers landed, now holds UMass Boston, which moved there in 1974, the John F. Kennedy Presidential Library, dedicated in 1979, the Edward M. Kennedy Institute and the Massachusetts Archives. The Fairmount Line gained new Dorchester stations at Talbot Avenue in November 2012 and Four Corners/Geneva in July 2013, and Pope John Paul II Park opened in 2001 on a former drive-in and dump along the Neponset. In May 2024 the Boston Planning Department began a Squares + Streets plan for Fields Corner, part of a citywide program covering housing, public space, small businesses and transportation in neighborhood centers; the department's project page showed it still in progress, with no adoption date.

housing.text: Dorchester's housing includes single-family, two-family and three-family houses and condominiums. Three-decker apartment buildings went up in large numbers alongside the streetcar lines from around 1890, and Victorian houses fill hills such as Savin Hill, where lots were sold after the Civil War. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2016-2020 American Community Survey counts 44,979 occupied housing units, 37.3% of them owner-occupied, compared with 35.3% citywide.

areas.name: Savin Hill
areas.line: A hill above Dorchester Bay, first called Rock Hill and renamed in 1819, built up with Victorian houses after the Civil War; it has a Red Line station from 1927 and Savin Hill and Malibu beaches nearby.

areas.name: Fields Corner
areas.line: A commercial district centered on the X-shaped crossing of Dorchester Avenue and Adams Street, named for Zechariah Field, with the 1874 Fields Corner Municipal Building and a Red Line station; side streets hold three-deckers and Victorian houses.

areas.name: Ashmont
areas.line: The area around Ashmont station at Dorchester Avenue and Ashmont Street, the Red Line's southern terminus on this branch and the transfer point to the Mattapan Line, with Peabody Square's shops beside it.

areas.name: Lower Mills
areas.line: The old mill village on the Neponset River at the Milton line, where the Walter Baker chocolate buildings, a major part of them built from 1868, now hold mixed industrial, retail and residential uses; the district was listed on the National Register in 1980.

areas.name: Uphams Corner
areas.line: The square where Columbia Road meets Dudley and Stoughton Streets, named for grocer Amos Upham, with the 1918 Strand Theatre, the 1634 North Burying Ground and a Fairmount Line station.

areas.name: Codman Square
areas.line: The crossing of Washington Street and Talbot Avenue, a National Register district since 1983 that includes the 1806 Second Church in Dorchester and the 1904 Codman Square branch library; Talbot Avenue station on the Fairmount Line is nearby.

commute.text: The Red Line's Ashmont branch has five stations in Dorchester, and at Ashmont it meets the Mattapan Line trolley, which stops at Cedar Grove in southern Dorchester. The Fairmount Line runs from South Station through Newmarket, Uphams Corner, Four Corners/Geneva and Talbot Avenue toward Readville. I-93, Route 203 and Route 28 (Blue Hill Avenue) cross the neighborhood, along with Gallivan Boulevard and Morton Street.

places.name: John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum
places.line: I. M. Pei's library on a 9.5-acre site at the tip of Columbia Point, beside UMass Boston, dedicated on October 20, 1979, with a glass and steel pavilion 115 feet high.

places.name: James Blake House
places.line: Built in 1661, a date confirmed by tree-ring dating in 2007, and described as the oldest surviving house in Boston; it stands at 735 Columbia Road in Edward Everett Square and is owned by the Dorchester Historical Society.

places.name: Pope John Paul II Park
places.line: A 66-acre DCR park on the Neponset River, opened in 2001 on the site of the Neponset Drive-In and the Hallet Street dump, with trails including the Lower Neponset River Trail.

places.name: Franklin Park
places.line: Olmsted's 485-acre park, Boston's largest open space, which connects Dorchester with Roxbury, Jamaica Plain, Mattapan and Roslindale; it holds the Franklin Park Zoo and the William Devine Golf Course.

places.name: Strand Theatre
places.line: A theater at Uphams Corner, opened in 1918 as one of the first built specifically for motion pictures.

places.name: Dorchester North Burying Ground
places.line: A burying ground at Uphams Corner dating to 1634, one of the oldest in the country.

places.name: Dorchester-Milton Lower Mills Industrial District
places.line: The Walter Baker chocolate complex on both banks of the Neponset, where chocolate was made from 1765 until 1965, now in mixed industrial, retail and residential use.

history.text: Settlers from the Mary and John landed at Columbia Point on June 17 and founded the town of Dorchester.
Dorchester held what is described as the first town meeting in what became the United States, on October 8.
Dr. James Baker and John Hannan began making chocolate at Lower Mills, the start of the Walter Baker company.
After a June 1869 vote, the rest of the town of Dorchester was annexed to Boston.

faq.q: What is the median home price in Dorchester?
faq.a: According to The Warren Group's MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town table, which lists Dorchester on its own row, the median single-family sale price for calendar year 2025 was $800,000, across 103 sales. In 2024 it was $730,000, across 110 sales. Much of Dorchester's housing is two- and three-family buildings and condominiums, which this single-family figure does not cover, and condo figures could not be read from the table.

Yes. The Fairmount Line stops at Uphams Corner, Four Corners/Geneva and Talbot Avenue in Dorchester on its way between South Station and Readville. The Red Line also has five Dorchester stations, from JFK/UMass to Ashmont.

Dorchester's commercial districts grew from its old village centers: Uphams Corner and Bowdoin/Geneva in the north, and Fields Corner, Codman Square, Peabody Square at Ashmont, Adams Village and Lower Mills in the south. Residential sections include Savin Hill, Jones Hill, Meeting House Hill, Ashmont Hill, Neponset, Port Norfolk, Popes Hill and Cedar Grove.

notes: Written 2026-10-22. Population: Boston Planning & Development Agency Research Division, 'Boston in Context: Neighborhoods, 2020 Decennial Census Redistricting Data and 2016-2020 American Community Survey' (April 2022), 'Population by Age Group' table, total 122,191 for Dorchester as one neighborhood (approximated with 2020 block groups; the report does not split North and South Dorchester and gives no planning-district figure). The agency's January 1, 2025 estimate is 123,056 (not used). Housing tenure from the same report (ACS 2016-2020). Housing types and the streetcar-suburb framing from Wikipedia's Dorchester article; 'around 1890' for streetcars and three-deckers from the Boston Preservation Alliance's 'A Short History of Boston's Triple Deckers' (https://bostonpreservation.org/news-item/short-history-bostons-triple-deckers), quoting Arthur Krim that the two 'collided in Dorchester' in 1890. Savin Hill post-Civil War lots from Wikipedia's Savin Hill article (which also says Savin Hill was listed on the National Register on May 9, 2003; not repeated because the listing's name and boundary were not confirmed). Areas: six sections are given instead of the brief's 2 to 4 because the task asked for Savin Hill, Fields Corner, Ashmont and Lower Mills plus others, and Dorchester is the city's largest neighborhood. Red Line station dates (1927 and 1928) from Wikipedia's Ashmont branch article; Ashmont address and Mattapan Line transfer from the MBTA stop page. Fairmount stations from the MBTA timetable; Dorchester location of Talbot Avenue (near Codman Square) and Four Corners/Geneva (Mount Bowdoin section, 171 Geneva Avenue) from their Wikipedia articles; Uphams Corner station from Wikipedia's Uphams Corner article. Wikipedia says Dorchester has five Fairmount stations but does not name them; Newmarket and Morton Street may be counted but their neighborhood was not confirmed, so only three are listed. The Mattapan Line stops in Dorchester beyond Ashmont and Cedar Grove were not confirmed. Highways and roads from Wikipedia's Dorchester article, listed as named there; which streets carry Route 203 was not confirmed. Annexation: Wikipedia gives January 3 in the text and January 4 in the infobox, so only the year is used. 'First town meeting' and 'first public elementary school' are Wikipedia's claims, attributed as 'described as'; the Mather School is not named as a current school to avoid any school characterization. JFK Library facts from jfklibrary.org; the Kennedy Institute (2015) and Massachusetts Archives from Wikipedia. Fields Corner Squares + Streets: launched May 14 and 18, 2024; the Planning Department page (https://www.bostonplans.org/fields-corner) shows no adoption date as of this session, and the department's December 31, 2024 news release (https://www.boston.gov/node/16267656) says recommendations were to be refined in 2025. Dorchester Park was left out because Wikipedia gives a conflicting founding date (1861) and Olmsted commission (1895) and the boston.gov page failed to load. Market: single-family row read twice in this session with identical YTD figures; condo table truncated at Brookline. Schools: assignment is by address and set by Boston Public Schools. Fair housing: Wikipedia's Fields Corner article describes the area by the national cuisine of its restaurants, and the Dorchester article covers the Columbia Point public housing project and demographic change; none of this was used. No section is characterized by who lives there, and no crime or change-over-time framing about residents is used. Wikipedia describes Victorian 'commuter bedroom communities'; only the built-form point (streetcar suburb) is kept. Fact-check 2026-10-22: verified more than 6 square miles, the bordering neighborhoods and Neponset/Quincy/Milton, North Dorchester's definition, the June 17, 1630 landing, the October 8, 1633 town meeting, the 1639 Mather School, the 1634 Stoughton mill, Walter Baker until 1965, the June 22, 1869 vote, the Old Colony Railroad in 1845, the commercial squares and residential sections, the housing mix (27.3% single-family, 23.1% two-family, 24.6% three-family, 25.0% condo units), Columbia Point institutions, the roads, and 'five Red Line, five Mattapan Line and five Fairmount Line stations' (Wikipedia); Fairmount stops in order (MBTA timetable); Uphams Corner, Four Corners/Geneva (Mount Bowdoin, opened July 1, 2013) and Talbot Avenue (near Codman Square, opened November 12, 2012) are each placed in Dorchester by their station articles; Morton Street is in Mattapan and Newmarket's neighborhood is not given, so the record keeps three Fairmount stations; Cedar Grove is in southern Dorchester; Red Line openings November 5, 1927 and September 1, 1928 (Ashmont branch article); Savin Hill, Fields Corner, Lower Mills (1765, 1868, NRHP 1980), Uphams Corner, Codman Square District (1983), James Blake House, Pope John Paul II Park (66 acres, 2001), JFK Library (jfklibrary.org), Franklin Park (city), Fields Corner Squares + Streets (launched May 14 and 18, 2024, no adoption shown); population 122,191 and tenure (BPDA April 2022). Market row checked against reading_1: YTD sales 110 to 103 and medians $730,000 to $800,000 match the fields and FAQ, and -6.4% and 9.6% agree. Corrected: the boundaries no longer list Mattapan as a western neighbor or say 'planners' divide North and South Dorchester (Wikipedia lists South Boston, Roxbury, Jamaica Plain, Hyde Park and the South End); the answer now says annexation came in stages ending in 1870; 'electric streetcars arrived around 1890' (no source says electric) is now the Preservation Alliance's point that the streetcar and three-decker came together in Dorchester by 1890, and the horsecar line is described as Wikipedia does; Lower Mills buildings are 'a major part' built from 1868; Franklin Park is described by the neighborhoods it connects, not as 'Dorchester's western edge'; the Mattapan Line 'runs along the Neponset' is replaced with its Cedar Grove stop; the Squares + Streets sentence no longer calls the program zoning reform for housing near transit (the project page does not). Fair housing: re-read every sentence; sections are described by streets, buildings and transit only. Wikipedia's Fields Corner list of resident groups, Savin Hill's gentrification and population lines and the Dorchester article's demographic content remain excluded.
